<reflection>
Low catalyst experiment shifted the leaderboard: M11, M16, M14, M9 (deactivation mechanisms) rise to the top by ~1.5 units over baseline mechanisms. This confirms some form of catalyst deactivation. Also, M3 became relatively competitive (5th place), suggesting non-trivial catalyst-order dependence may exist. M20 still very bad.

Top cluster: M11 (S+cat→inactive), M16 (S+catS→inactive), M14 (catS→inactive), M9 (cat→inactive). These four all involve deactivation but by different pathways:
- M9: spontaneous cat deactivation (rate ∝ [cat])
- M11: S-driven cat deactivation (rate ∝ [S][cat])
- M14: spontaneous catS deactivation (rate ∝ [catS])
- M16: S-driven catS deactivation (rate ∝ [S][catS])
</hypothesis>

<hypothesis>
To distinguish M9, M11, M14, M16, I need to change [S] while keeping [cat] similar. The key difference:
- M9: deactivation independent of [S] → extent of deactivation is time-based
- M11: deactivation ∝ [S] → higher [S] gives faster deactivation
- M14: deactivation ∝ [catS] which saturates with [S] → mildly dependent on [S]
- M16: deactivation ∝ [S][catS] → strong [S] dependence

Best experiment: HIGH substrate concentration (say 4.0 M), same catalyst (0.01 M), no product.

Predictions:
- M9: same absolute deactivation regardless of [S] → conversion nearly complete before deactivation matters if V is high enough
- M11: much faster catalyst death (4x [S]) → early plateau at low conversion (worst outcome for reaching high conversion)
- M14: intermediate; catS saturates so deactivation similar to baseline; final conversion moderate
- M16: strong [S]-driven deactivation; early plateau
- M3 (cat2 formation): faster with more S consumed early
- M7 (catS2): high [S] favors catS2 formation which slows things
- M12, M17: not [S]-driven so less affected

This should discriminate M9 vs M11/M14/M16 vs M14/M16 distinctions.
</hypothesis>
